# Morning Memo for 2026-08-30

Source failures: `github-trending-weekly` reported `No fetcher for type: github_trending`. `reddit-localllama` returned HTTP 429 during fetch.

Backfill note: most surfaced items in this batch are older late-May items that appear to have landed as fresh ingest now, not same-day news. Treat them as backlog signals, not as this morning's launches.

## Worth attention

- **Supabase on npm supply-chain attacks**: Supabase published a blunt checklist for surviving the current npm threat model, especially if agents install packages for you. The practical moves are the ones that matter: release-age gates, no default install scripts, exact pins for sensitive dependencies, SHA-pinned GitHub Actions, and no `pull_request_target` flows that touch PR code. If you maintain Node repos, this is worth turning into an audit list now rather than after the next poisoned dependency.

- **Vercel's inference-theft warning**: Vercel described a real attack pattern where public AI endpoints get wrapped behind an OpenAI-compatible proxy and resold, turning one cheap bypass into a large model bill. The core lesson is broader than the product pitch: per-session auth and IP limits are not enough when the attacker can amortize them across thousands of inference calls. If you expose any AI endpoint, move your verification logic onto each request path.

- **AI Gateway provider allowlists**: Vercel added team-wide provider allowlists that enforce approved model vendors at the gateway layer, including BYOK traffic. That matters because agent-side preferences can no longer quietly bypass central policy, and new providers stay off by default once the allowlist is enabled. Even if you do not use Vercel, the pattern is right: keep provider policy server-side and auditable.

- **Vercel function billing changed shape**: Function invocations are moving from package-based pricing to per-unit pricing for Pro and new Enterprise customers starting next billing cycle. The headline rate stays close to the old economics, but the packaging shift means teams should re-check how invocation-heavy workloads map to spend, especially if you relied on included-credit behavior or shared-team usage assumptions.

- **MCP 2026-07-28 release candidate**: The MCP project published a release candidate and explicitly said the spec is not final and version negotiation still matters. That is the kind of protocol transition where clients and servers start failing in confusing ways if one side silently treats the newest draft as settled. If you build MCP tooling, treat this as a compatibility checkpoint and keep negotiation paths tested.

- **CPython now officially supports RISC-V**: RISC-V reached official tier-3 support in CPython, backed by ongoing testing on real hardware and a path toward better CI coverage. It is not a mainstream workflow shift tomorrow, but it does materially improve the odds that Python-on-RISC-V issues get handled upstream instead of lingering as best-effort side work.
